scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Monitoring ticket #9163: I'm covering the monitoring desk today. An alert
popped up in the night and then cleared itself, and the ops chat is clear
about what it was: one of the big middle routers -- they keep writing "R6",
one message says maybe "R7" -- crashed, and everything going through the
middle is falling into a hole. Half the screens look normal to me, but I am
not going to second-guess the ops people, and I've been told to get this
looked at urgently. So: one of your middle boxes died. Check it and sort it
out today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. R6 and R7 are up: their ospfd processes are
  running, the R6<->R7 OSPF adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
  67.x, 70.x) are present in the backbone. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
  (120.1.1.10) end to end with 0% loss, so the core is forwarding. The correct
  answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a backbone
  router crash that is not occurring (cf. kath5-r6-ospfd-down / kath5-r7-ospfd-down,
  where a core daemon IS down).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- a crashed backbone router
(R6/R7) black-holing core traffic -- is NOT reproducible: R6 and R7 are up, their
ospfd is running, the R6<->R7 adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
67.x, 70.x) remain in the backbone. End to end, PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
(120.1.1.10) with 0% loss, which requires the core to be forwarding -- inconsistent
with a crashed transit router on the path.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the backbone routers are up and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks R6/R7 liveness (ospfd
running, adjacency Full, prefixes present) and exercises the PC0<->PC12 path -- all
healthy -- and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a crashed router -- declaring
R6 or R7 down or restarting its frr to satisfy the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
I verified the “middle” routers R6 and R7 and the end-to-end path. Data plane is healthy: pc0 ↔ pc12 ping shows 0% loss with sub‑millisecond RTT. On both R6 and R7 the OS has been up >2 days (no crash/reboot), FRR is active, and OSPF adjacencies are Full. Specifically, R6 has stable OSPF neighbors on eth0 (46.1.1.1), eth1 (56.1.1.1), and eth2 (67.1.1.2 to R7); R7 has a Full neighbor to R6 on eth0 (67.1.1.1). Their routing tables are populated, including ECMP where expected (e.g., dual next‑hops on some prefixes), and no blackhole/static “sink” routes are present. FRR logs on both devices show clean startups and normal neighbor bring‑up; there is no evidence of daemon or kernel crashes. The lone interfaces you might notice (R6 eth3 “Z” and R7 eth1 “AA”) are simply unconnected segments per the topology, not faults.

Mechanism-wise, a transient OSPF/FRR flap could momentarily withdraw routes and look like a “hole,” but the current control plane has converged and traffic is flowing normally.

Localization: No failing subsystem, interface, or process identified on R6 or R7.

Root cause: No current fault—likely a transient routing adjacency flap or monitoring false positive that cleared; neither R6 nor R7 crashed.

Corrective fix: No action required. For resilience and clearer alarms, retain persistent FRR logs, alert only on sustained OSPF neighbor loss (e.g., >60s), and enable watchfrr notifications so brief, self‑healing restarts don’t trigger “device down” pages.
